connection: Every later session assumes you already understand how TimeClock.sln, src/, and tests/ came to exist. This session scaffolds that layout yourself with the dotnet CLI, so the structure is something you built, not something you found.
objectives: Use dotnet new to generate a solution, a class library, a console app, and an xUnit test project.
Explain why source projects live under src/ and test projects live under tests/.
Use dotnet sln add and dotnet add reference to wire projects into a solution and into each other.
Explain why TimeClock.App references TimeClock.Domain but TimeClock.Domain does not reference TimeClock.App.

visuals.title: A solution is a list of projects, not a project itself
visuals.explanation: TimeClock.sln does not contain code. It is a manifest that names which .csproj files belong together so one command can build or test all of them.

visuals.title: dotnet new turns a template name into a folder
visuals.explanation: dotnet new classlib -o src/TimeClock.Domain creates a folder containing TimeClock.Domain.csproj and a starter .cs file. The -o path is also where the project will live.

visuals.title: Scaffold, wire, build — in that order
visuals.explanation: Generate the project, add it to the solution, add any project references it needs, then build. Doing these out of order produces confusing errors that look like missing code.

visuals.title: A test project is a project, with one extra reference
visuals.explanation: TimeClock.Domain.Tests is an ordinary class library plus the xUnit package and a ProjectReference to the code it tests. Nothing about it is structurally special.

options: Compiled C# code for the whole application
A list of project paths and build configurations, no source code
preQuiz.explanation: A .sln file is a manifest. The code lives entirely inside the .csproj-owning folders it lists.

preQuiz.prompt: Why does TimeClock.App's .csproj have a ProjectReference to TimeClock.Domain, but TimeClock.Domain's .csproj has no reference back to TimeClock.App?
options: Domain is a reusable library; App is one consumer of it, and a library should not depend on any particular consumer
preQuiz.explanation: If Domain referenced App, you could never reuse Domain in a second consumer (like a future TimeClock.Web) without dragging App along. The dependency points from the specific thing toward the general thing, never the reverse.

preQuiz.prompt: You create a project with dotnet new classlib but never run dotnet sln add. What happens when you run dotnet build TimeClock.sln?
options: The new project builds along with the others automatically
The new project is silently skipped — the solution only builds what it's told to include
preQuiz.explanation: Folder presence is not membership. A project only participates in solution-wide build/test/restore once it's listed inside the .sln file.

concept.title: dotnet new generates a project, not an app
paragraphs: Every dotnet new <template> command does the same two things: it creates a folder (or uses -o to name one), and it drops a .csproj file plus a minimal starter source file into it. classlib gives you a library with no entry point. console gives you an executable with a Main. xunit gives you a test project pre-wired with the xUnit and test-SDK package references.

Nothing about running dotnet new touches a solution file. The project exists as a standalone, buildable unit the moment it's created — dotnet build src/TimeClock.Domain/TimeClock.Domain.csproj would already work. A solution is a separate, later step that groups projects together.
concept.code:
dotnet new classlib -o src/TimeClock.Domain
dotnet new console -o src/TimeClock.App
dotnet new xunit -o tests/TimeClock.Domain.Tests

concept.title: src/ and tests/ are convention, not a compiler rule
paragraphs: Nothing in the .NET toolchain requires a src/ or tests/ folder. TimeClock.sln groups its projects under a src solution folder and a tests solution folder purely so dotnet sln list and any IDE's solution explorer show the same two-way split a human would draw by hand: things that ship, and things that check the things that ship.

The real payoff of the convention shows up at scale. tests/TimeClock.Domain.Tests.csproj references ..\..\src\TimeClock.Domain\TimeClock.Domain.csproj — a relative path that only stays short and stable because both sides of the split are always exactly one folder deep.
concept.code:
dotnet new sln -n TimeClock
dotnet sln TimeClock.sln add src/TimeClock.Domain/TimeClock.Domain.csproj
dotnet sln TimeClock.sln add src/TimeClock.App/TimeClock.App.csproj
dotnet sln TimeClock.sln add tests/TimeClock.Domain.Tests/TimeClock.Domain.Tests.csproj

concept.title: Project references encode dependency direction
paragraphs: dotnet add <project> reference <other-project> edits the first project's .csproj to add a <ProjectReference> pointing at the second. That's the entire mechanism — no magic, just an XML element the compiler uses to find the other assembly's public types.

The direction you choose is a design decision. TimeClock.App references TimeClock.Domain because the console app is one specific consumer of the domain's types (ClockEntry, PayrollService). TimeClock.Domain never references TimeClock.App back — a reusable library that reached into its own consumer's code would only be reusable by that one consumer. Later sessions add TimeClock.Infrastructure and TimeClock.Web; both will point at Domain for the same reason, and neither will point at App.
concept.code:
dotnet add src/TimeClock.App/TimeClock.App.csproj reference src/TimeClock.Domain/TimeClock.Domain.csproj
dotnet add tests/TimeClock.Domain.Tests/TimeClock.Domain.Tests.csproj reference src/TimeClock.Domain/TimeClock.Domain.csproj

lab.objective: Reproduce TimeClock's actual project layout from scratch using the dotnet CLI, then confirm your scratch solution matches the real one.
lab.startingCondition: The repository already contains a working TimeClock.sln with TimeClock.Domain, TimeClock.App, and TimeClock.Domain.Tests (plus TimeClock.Infrastructure and TimeClock.Web, introduced in later sessions). You will rebuild the first three from nothing in a separate scratch folder — you will not modify the repository's own solution in this lab.
steps: In a new empty scratch folder outside this repository, run: dotnet new sln -n TimeClock
Run: dotnet new classlib -o src/TimeClock.Domain, then dotnet new console -o src/TimeClock.App, then dotnet new xunit -o tests/TimeClock.Domain.Tests
Add all three to the solution with dotnet sln TimeClock.sln add for each .csproj path
Wire references: dotnet add src/TimeClock.App reference src/TimeClock.Domain, and dotnet add tests/TimeClock.Domain.Tests reference src/TimeClock.Domain
Run dotnet build TimeClock.sln in your scratch folder and confirm all three projects build

From the real repository root, run dotnet sln TimeClock.sln list and compare its project list and paths against what you just built — the App/Domain/Tests portion should match exactly; Infrastructure and Web are covered later
lab.expectedBehavior: Your scratch solution builds three projects with zero errors. dotnet sln TimeClock.sln list against the real repository shows src\TimeClock.Domain\TimeClock.Domain.csproj, src\TimeClock.App\TimeClock.App.csproj, and tests\TimeClock.Domain.Tests\TimeClock.Domain.Tests.csproj at the same relative paths and depth you just recreated.

commit: session-01: scaffold the solution with dotnet new, dotnet sln add, and dotnet add reference
review: The scratch solution builds all three projects without errors.
TimeClock.App's .csproj contains a ProjectReference to TimeClock.Domain; TimeClock.Domain's .csproj contains none.
The scratch project list matches the real repository's App/Domain/Tests projects at the same relative paths.
Every command was run against explicit project or solution paths, not relied on ambient defaults.

postQuiz.prompt: You run dotnet new console -o src/TimeClock.App but never run dotnet sln add. Later, dotnet build TimeClock.sln succeeds with no mention of TimeClock.App. Why?
options: Console apps build automatically once created
TimeClock.App was never added to the solution, so the solution build has no reason to know it exists
dotnet build always finds every .csproj under the current directory
postQuiz.explanation: A folder on disk and a solution member are two different things. Only dotnet sln add creates the membership dotnet build TimeClock.sln relies on.

postQuiz.prompt: If you accidentally added a ProjectReference from TimeClock.Domain to TimeClock.App, what would break first?
options: A future second consumer of Domain (like TimeClock.Web) would compile Domain, and transitively compile all of App's code too, even though it never asked for App
The solution file would fail to parse
postQuiz.explanation: A reference pulls in everything the referenced project needs to compile. A library referencing its own consumer forces every future consumer to drag that first consumer along.

postQuiz.prompt: Why does tests/TimeClock.Domain.Tests reference src/TimeClock.Domain directly, rather than going through TimeClock.App?
options: Test projects can only reference libraries, never executables
The tests exist to verify Domain's behavior specifically, so they should depend on exactly the code under test and nothing extra
App and Domain are actually the same project
postQuiz.explanation: Referencing only what you're testing keeps the dependency graph honest — the tests would still compile even if App were deleted entirely.

reflections: Which command created files on disk, and which command changed what dotnet build TimeClock.sln considers in scope?
Why does the reference arrow point from App to Domain and never the reverse?
What would you have to do differently if you wanted a second console app to also use TimeClock.Domain?
whatBreaks: Skipping dotnet sln add leaves a project that builds standalone but is invisible to solution-wide build/test/restore commands. Skipping dotnet add reference leaves TimeClock.App unable to resolve ClockEntry or any other Domain type, and the compiler reports it as a missing type rather than a missing reference — a genuinely confusing error if you don't already know references are the fix. Reversing the reference direction (Domain referencing App) would compile today but would block every future project, like TimeClock.Infrastructure or TimeClock.Web, from depending on Domain without also depending on App.
summary: A solution is a manifest naming which projects build and test together; it is created and populated with dotnet new, dotnet sln add, and dotnet add reference, three separate, ordinary CLI commands with no hidden magic. The src/ and tests/ split and the one-way App-to-Domain reference are both deliberate choices, not defaults the tooling forces on you.
